For all the political theater that defines Washington, few failures are as routine—or as damaging—as Congress’s inability to pass defense funding on time. In 13 of the last 14 fiscal years, the Department of Defense has been forced to limp along under temporary “continuing resolutions.” These stopgaps keep the lights on but stall planning, freeze innovation, and waste billions in uncertainty.

This is not a left or right issue; it’s a governance issue. The men and women serving in uniform deserve budgets that arrive on time and reflect deliberation, not dysfunction. Predictability in defense spending should be the floor of competence in Congress, not the ceiling.

The Defense Funding Accountability Act of 2026 offers a practical fix. It doesn’t reinvent government—it simply enforces the deadlines and accountability measures that every responsible organization already lives by.

⸻

A Modest, Sensible Proposal

1. Timelines with Teeth
The bill requires the Armed Services Committees to report the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) by June 1, with both chambers passing their versions by July 31. A final compromise bill would be signed into law by August 31, and appropriations completed by September 30. These are not radical demands—they mirror timelines Congress has occasionally met when discipline prevailed.

2. An Automatic Safety Net
If lawmakers miss the September 30 deadline, an automatic continuing resolution would keep the Pentagon funded at last year’s levels, trimmed by 1% to discourage complacency. This safeguard protects troops and taxpayers alike: readiness doesn’t lapse, but procrastination still carries a cost.

3. Accountability Where It Matters
Starting October 1, members of Congress who fail to complete their work would have their pay withheld until the NDAA and appropriations bills are enacted—permanently forfeited if delays stretch past 30 days. No recesses longer than three days would be allowed during the impasse, and the Government Accountability Office would publish public reports naming the committees and leaders responsible for delays.

⸻

Good Governance, Not Punishment

The bill would amend the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act and the Antideficiency Act, tightening the process without undermining congressional authority. Waivers would require a two-thirds vote, ensuring only genuine emergencies justify exceptions.

The point isn’t to shame Congress—it’s to restore trust. The military can’t plan in 30-day increments. Defense contractors can’t sign multi-year agreements based on guesswork. Taxpayers shouldn’t fund a system that rewards paralysis.

⸻

A Bipartisan Obligation

Republicans and Democrats alike lament the chaos of continuing resolutions, but lamentation has become its own form of inertia. This bill offers something rarer than outrage: a path to reform grounded in realism.

The Defense Funding Accountability Act doesn’t demand heroism—just responsibility. It reminds lawmakers that leadership means meeting deadlines, and that national security shouldn’t hinge on brinkmanship. In an era when faith in government feels like a relic, this small act of discipline could restore something larger: the belief that Congress can, on occasion, still do its job.
